strengths: The paper studies a useful fixed-confidence multi-objective Bayesian-optimization problem on large or continuous domains. Combining adaptive tree refinement with Pareto-set identification is well motivated and relevant to both Bayesian-optimization and bandit-theory audiences.

Adaptive ε-PAL is described through explicit modeling, discarding, covering, and refinement rules. The pseudocode, illustrations, and notation table make the main algorithmic ideas reasonably accessible despite their technicality.

Providing both information-gain and metric-dimension perspectives is potentially valuable, especially because the formulation permits correlated GP objectives. The appendix represents a substantial effort toward correctness and sample-complexity guarantees.

The experiments compare against several established MOBO methods, use repeated functions and noise realizations, and expose a practically meaningful accuracy-runtime tradeoff through the maximum tree depth.
weaknesses: [Necessary] The main theorem is not well-defined as written. Definition 11 quantifies over every r>0; for any positive dimension its right-hand side becomes negative as r grows, so even [0,1] does not have the claimed finite metric dimension under this definition. Moreover, V_h contains log(h²) although the tree starts at h=0, making V_0 undefined. The scale range and level indexing must be corrected throughout the dependent results.

[Necessary] A key step in the metric-dimension proof is unsupported. Lemma 14 infers β_{τ_t}^{1/2}‖σ_{τ_t}(parent)‖≤‖V_{h-1}‖ merely because the parent was refined at an earlier time. Since β increases, the refinement-time inequality need not persist, and the argument is also undefined for the root. This lemma feeds directly into Lemma 15, Proposition 5, and Theorem 1; a new proof, perhaps using the inherited cumulative rectangle with a separate root analysis, is required.

[Necessary] Proposition 1 does not establish the claimed linear-information example under the paper's compact setting. Its Ω(T) conclusion requires nonvanishing bump amplitudes, which yields infinitely many canonically separated points; Assumption 1 then forces them to remain separated under d, contradicting compactness. With decaying amplitudes, the displayed lower bound need not be Ω(T). In addition, after applying a general mixing matrix A, the posterior marginal variance is a weighted sum over amplitudes, not the single amplitude substituted in the proof. Consequently, the claimed non-comparability of the two bounds remains unsupported.

[Necessary] Other proof defects collectively require a careful audit: the stopping arguments in Propositions 4 and 5 do not logically derive Pr(τ_s>T)=0 from the stated event implication; Proposition 3 does not control the dependence of β on total rather than node-specific evaluations; Lemma 11 asserts positive definiteness where only semidefiniteness is guaranteed; the Voronoi cells need not be disjoint under the stated tie convention; and g in Lemma 5 is undefined.

[Necessary] The empirical evidence is too limited for the broad outperformance and efficiency claims. It covers only one one-dimensional, two-objective, prior-matched synthetic setup. More importantly, Table 2 reports the arithmetic average of accuracy and coverage rather than either quantity separately, so it cannot demonstrate that both requirements of an ε-accurate set hold. The conversion of the returned union of cells into evaluated prediction points is also unspecified. At minimum, report both metrics separately and narrow the claims; an adaptive-versus-uniform ablation and a working finite ε-PAL comparison would directly test the proposed contribution.

[Optional] Reproducibility and presentation would benefit from releasing the Adaptive ε-PAL implementation, specifying all constants, hardware, runtime aggregation, baseline surrogate settings, and confidence-interval calculation. Numerous smaller notation and prose errors—including the claim that a polynomial-in-T bound decreases exponentially—should also be corrected.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a well-motivated problem—fixed-confidence Pareto-set identification over potentially infinite design spaces—with an identifiable audience in Bayesian optimization and active learning. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-v_6r9m7f/call-70f466dc1efc48068aa9f3c5ac40d690/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Adaptive ε-PAL combines tree-based adaptive discretization with cumulative multi-output GP confidence rectangles and region-level discard, covering, refinement, and evaluation rules. This is an interesting conceptual extension beyond finite grids.

The intended theory is ambitious and potentially useful: it offers both information-gain and metric-dimension sample-complexity bounds and attempts to account for dependence among objectives through the joint covariance.

The main exposition provides useful intuition, diagrams, pseudocode, and a notation table. The experiments include several established MOBO baselines and expose the substantial accuracy/runtime tradeoff caused by the tree-depth parameter.
weaknesses: Necessary: Theorem 1 is not established by the supplied proof. As printed, V_h is undefined at h=0 because it contains log(h²); Corollary 1 has inconsistent covering-number exponents and sums h^{-2} starting at h=0; Lemma 14 applies a refinement inequality using the current, larger β_τ although it was only known at the earlier refinement time; and the root case is untreated. Most directly, Propositions 4 and 5 conclude P(τ_s>T)=0 merely from the implication {τ_s=T}⇒{ω_{t_s}<ε}, which does not logically yield the claimed sample-complexity bound. These central gaps require a corrected theorem and proof, not just copyediting.

Necessary: Proposition 1 does not convincingly establish the claimed linear-information-gain example under Assumption 1. The required metric is only asserted. Nonvanishing amplitudes, which are needed for Ω(T), create infinitely many points separated in the GP metric and appear incompatible with compactness of d together with l_j≤C_k d^α. The construction also omits x=0 from its interval partition, and the text incorrectly describes a polynomial-in-T dimension bound as decreasing exponentially.

Necessary: The algorithm is not specified self-consistently. Algorithm 1 computes the pessimistic Pareto set from R_t before R_t is constructed, its first observation is indexed y_0 despite observations starting at one, and the prose gives an invalid child-index range. Definition 10's closed Voronoi cells can overlap at ties despite being called a partition. These issues should be corrected and the implementation shown to match the corrected specification.

Necessary: The broad empirical superiority claim is supported by only one synthetic setting with one-dimensional inputs, two independent GP objectives, and one kernel/noise configuration. It does not test the emphasized dependent-objective setting, higher-dimensional scaling, or adaptive versus uniform discretization directly; the closest ε-PAL baseline is absent. Either substantially broaden the evidence or narrow the abstract and conclusions to this specific experiment.

Necessary: Table 2 averages accuracy and coverage into one number, potentially concealing a serious precision/coverage imbalance; both metrics should be reported separately. The five runs on each of only ten shared functions also require hierarchical uncertainty accounting. It is unclear how the uncountable returned cell union was discretized, how each baseline's predicted set and GP hyperparameters were constructed, or what hardware and software versions were used. MSE and runtime have no uncertainty estimates.

Necessary: The practical efficiency conclusion relies on depth-capped variants that set V_h=0 beyond h_max and therefore do not retain the stated confidence guarantee. Meanwhile, the theoretically parameterized variant takes over 15 hours on the very small one-dimensional problem. This distinction must be explicit and the practical modification separately analyzed or presented strictly as an unguaranteed heuristic.

Optional: Correct the duplicate runtime paragraph, the positive-definite claim in Lemma 11 where only semidefiniteness is assured, the definition of maximum information gain as a maximization over observations rather than design sequences, and numerous indexing and prose errors. The recommendation is driven by unresolved evidential validity, not by a conference-style novelty or significance threshold; the core idea has a plausible path to acceptance after rigorous repair.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-jmn99huj/call-625f0b3c69c740e3a248e7b166821c89/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an identifiable problem of interest: fixed-confidence Pareto-set identification over large or continuous design spaces, including correlated GP objectives.

The region-level confidence rectangles and discard/cover/refine mechanism are a natural, potentially useful integration of Pareto active learning with adaptive discretization. The intuition, pseudocode, figures, and complexity discussion make the main idea reasonably understandable.

Providing both information-gain and metric-dimension analyses is conceptually valuable because the two can capture different aspects of problem difficulty. The extensive appendix attempts to state all assumptions and supply an end-to-end correctness argument.

The experiment includes modern baselines, 10 sampled functions with five runs each, multiple quality metrics, and runtime measurements. The comparison of theoretical and truncated tree depths also exposes an important computational tradeoff.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central sample-complexity theorem is not established by the present proof. Among several concrete problems, V₀ is undefined because its formula contains log(h²) at h=0; the root uses an undefined parent; Lemma 11 incorrectly claims that K_x(K+Σ)⁻¹K_xᵀ is positive definite when it can be singular or zero; and Lemma 14 applies the parent's refinement inequality using the current, larger β although that inequality held at an earlier round. The final arguments in Propositions 4 and 5—asserting that {τ_s=T} implies Pr(τ_s>T)=0—also do not follow without a bound valid at every evaluation prefix. These gaps require corrected statements and proofs, not just typographical cleanup.

Necessary: The notation in the dimension bound is internally inconsistent. K₁ contains β_{τ_s} in Lemma 15, is called a constant, disappears as a separate β factor in Proposition 5, and then reappears as K₁β_T in Theorem 1. The termination proof likewise assumes, without controlling the relation between a node's evaluation count and the global evaluation index, that its confidence term must eventually fall below the refinement threshold.

Necessary: Proposition 1's claimed Ω(T) information gain is unsupported. Its displayed lower bound is linear only if the sequence ā_{Tj} stays bounded away from zero, which is never imposed. Such a choice also conflicts with the required compact/Hölder setting for the independent points x_i→0; the construction does not even define the asserted partition at 0. The statement that the metric-dimension expression decreases “exponentially” in T is also false—it decreases polynomially up to logarithms. This proposition should be repaired rigorously or removed.

Necessary: The empirical ε-accuracy test is not equivalent to membership in Z_ε as claimed. A point arbitrarily far below a Pareto point still satisfies f(x)≼_εf(x*), so the stated operational test can count very poor points as accurate. Moreover, Table 2 reports only the average of accuracy and coverage rather than the two quantities separately. The precise implementation must be documented and the results recomputed with a valid set-accuracy test and separately reported coverage.

Necessary: The broad empirical claims are not supported by one one-dimensional, two-objective, independent-GP setting. There is no correlated-objective experiment despite that being a highlighted contribution, no higher-dimensional or higher-objective case, and no adaptive-versus-uniform ablation. The direct predecessor ε-PAL is excluded after unexplained nontermination. Additional evidence is needed, or the outperformance and adaptive-discretization claims must be narrowed to the tested synthetic setting.

The fast h_max=9 and h_max=10 variants set V_h=0 at the depth cap, which invalidates the within-cell variation event used by the guarantee. Their speed should therefore be presented explicitly as heuristic performance, distinct from the certified algorithm; notably, the theoretically parameterized variant takes over 15 hours on the simple test. Optional improvements include releasing the implementation and configurations, reporting equal-budget learning curves, and correcting indexing, figure-caption, and repeated-text errors.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important problem—fixed-confidence Pareto-set identification over large or continuous design spaces—with an identifiable audience in Bayesian optimization and active learning. This assessment covers the full manuscript and appendices: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ic1g82b0/call-1cb665ca61ed4bd3a99d4fcadfc5be77/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The adaptive-discretization construction is well motivated: region-wise confidence rectangles, separate discard/cover decisions, and the refine-versus-evaluate rule form a coherent algorithmic framework for avoiding an exhaustive grid.

Pursuing both information-gain and metric-dimension sample-complexity bounds is valuable, particularly because the formulation permits dependent GP outputs. The extensive appendix shows substantial effort toward a self-contained analysis.
The high-level exposition, pseudocode, notation table, and conceptual figures generally make a technically complicated method understandable.
The experiments include several established MOBO baselines, give competitors larger evaluation budgets, and expose the substantial accuracy/runtime trade-off induced by the maximum tree depth.
weaknesses: Necessary: The main sample-complexity theorem is not established by the proofs as written. Lemma 3 provides a sufficient condition for termination, but Propositions 4 and 5 use it in the reverse direction and conclude Pr(τ_s>T)=0 from an implication involving τ_s=T; that conclusion does not follow. Lemma 14 also assumes that β_{τ_t}^{1/2}σ_{τ_t} at a parent still satisfies the refinement inequality at a later round merely because the parent was refined earlier, although β grows with time. A corrected stopping-time argument and a valid replacement for this later-time inequality are required.

Necessary: Proposition 1 does not prove γ_T=Ω(T). Its displayed lower bound is proportional to T times a quantity involving the possibly vanishing amplitudes ā_{Tj}, so positivity and monotonicity alone do not yield a uniform linear lower bound. After applying the mixing matrix A, the marginal variance is a weighted sum, not ā_{ij}² as subsequently substituted. Moreover, satisfaction of the compactness/Hölder assumption is only asserted via a ‘suitably chosen metric’; amplitudes bounded away from zero would create infinitely many GP-metric-separated points, apparently conflicting with that assumption. This proposition and the claim that neither bound dominates require a new valid construction or removal.

Necessary: Several formal definitions are literally ill-defined or false as stated. V_h contains log(h²) while being defined at h=0; the metric-dimension inequality is required for every r>0, which fails for positive dimension when r becomes arbitrarily large; closed Voronoi cells need tie-breaking to form a partition; maximum information gain is maximized over observations rather than design sequences; and Lemma 11 claims positive definiteness where only positive semidefiniteness is guaranteed. Some are locally repairable, but they currently prevent the theorem from being read as a rigorous result. The dependence of K_1 and K_2 on τ_s in Lemma 15 must also be reconciled with Theorem 1's description of them as T-independent constants/functions.

Necessary: The empirical success criteria are not clearly aligned with Definitions 3–5. Saying that a predicted point is ε-dominated by a true Pareto point is not an operational test of membership in Z_ε under the paper's ordering—it can hold for arbitrarily poor dominated points—and the stated 2ε ‘equivalences’ do not follow. It is also unspecified how the algorithm's union of continuous cells becomes the finite predicted set used in Tables 2–3. Accuracy and coverage should be defined unambiguously, implemented in the correct directions, and reported separately rather than only through their average; the fraction of runs satisfying the complete set-level event would be the relevant check of the high-probability guarantee.

Necessary: The broad empirical claim of outperforming competing Pareto-set methods is supported by only one favorable synthetic setting: one input dimension, two independent objectives, functions sampled from the known model, and ten underlying functions. The closest fixed-confidence baseline, ε-PAL, is omitted, and there is no matched uniform-discretization ablation isolating the benefit of adaptivity. The claim should be narrowed to this experiment unless substantially broader evidence is added; evaluation counts and returned-set cardinalities should also be reported for fair comparison.

Necessary for reproducibility: The manuscript does not provide its own implementation or enough detail to reconstruct the experimental output sets, theoretical constants used to obtain h_max=24, confidence-interval calculation for the nested 10-functions-by-5-seeds design, or runtime environment. These omissions make the numerical evidence difficult to verify.

Optional: Once the correctness issues are resolved, higher-dimensional, correlated-output, misspecified-kernel, and standard benchmark experiments—plus node-count/memory scaling and guidance for choosing h_max—would make the practical contribution much more informative, but these extensions are not intrinsically required if the empirical claims are appropriately narrowed.

The combination of adaptive tree discretization, region-level confidence rectangles, and Pareto elimination is technically interesting and addresses a real limitation of finite-grid PAL methods.
Providing both information-gain and metric-dimension analyses is potentially useful; the multi-output formulation also allows posterior dependence between objectives.
The high-level motivation, algorithmic phases, pseudocode, and illustrations are generally understandable, and the extensive appendix exposes the proof strategy for scrutiny.
The experiment offers preliminary evidence that adaptive depth can trade computational cost against front quality and includes several recognizable MOBO baselines.
weaknesses: Necessary: The algorithm and theorem are not formally well-defined as written. At the root, p(x₀,₁) and V₋₁ are undefined, while V₀ contains log(h²) at h=0. Definition 11 and Lemma 1 also require a covering-number bound for every r>0; this is impossible for positive dimension because the covering number remains one for radii above the diameter while Qr^(-D) tends to zero. These statements need corrected domains and an explicit root convention.

Necessary: Important steps in the sample-complexity proof are invalid or incomplete. In Propositions 4 and 5, the fact that {τ_s=T} implies a small terminal width does not imply P(τ_s>T)=0; a prefix argument conditioned on reaching the T-th evaluation is required. Proposition 3 does not justify termination while β depends on the growing global evaluation count. Other errors include claiming a generally singular covariance product is positive definite in Lemma 11 and using an unjustified conditional-entropy comparison in Lemma 5. A careful end-to-end proof audit is needed before Theorem 1 can support the paper's main claims.

Necessary: Proposition 1 does not establish its claimed linear information gain under Assumption 1. Its displayed lower bound is Ω(T) only if the amplitudes remain bounded away from zero, but then the constructed points remain separated in the GP canonical metric, conflicting with compactness of d together with l_j≤C_k d^α. If the amplitudes decay to restore compactness, the given bound is o(T). The calculation after mixing by A also replaces the actual marginal variance with an individual amplitude without the required restriction. This proposition should be replaced, substantially revised, or its associated claims removed.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem and presents an interesting integration of tree-based adaptive discretization with GP confidence regions for Pareto-set identification over continuous spaces.

The central result is potentially valuable: it gives both information-gain and metric-dimension sample-complexity bounds, while allowing dependence between objectives. The extensive appendix makes the intended proof strategy inspectable.

The algorithm is explained through intuition, pseudocode, figures, and computational-complexity analysis. The work has a clear audience among researchers in Bayesian optimization and pure exploration.
The experiments compare against several established MOBO methods, use repeated trials, and report approximation quality and runtime, including a useful sensitivity study of maximum tree depth.
weaknesses: Necessary: Proposition 1 is not established as stated. Its linear-information-gain conclusion requires the amplitudes at the sampled locations to remain bounded away from zero, which is not assumed. Moreover, infinitely many independent locations with nonvanishing variance form an infinite separated set in the GP-induced metric, apparently conflicting with the compact, finite-dimensional metric setting under the stated Hölder relation. The unspecified claim that a “suitably chosen metric” resolves this is insufficient. The proposition and the advertised non-dominance of the two bounds should be proved under all setup assumptions or removed/narrowed. The subsequent statement that the metric-dimension quantity decreases exponentially in T is also incorrect; the displayed rate is polynomial up to logarithms.

Necessary: Several gaps remain in the proof of the main result. Lemma 11 incorrectly calls k_[T](x)(K_[T]+Sigma_[T])^{-1}k_[T](x)^T positive definite—it can be singular, although positive semidefiniteness may suffice. Propositions 4 and 5 do not justify Pr(tau_s>T)=0 from the stated implication involving tau_s=T. Proposition 3 similarly asserts the existence of a refinement time without controlling the growth of beta relative to visits to a node, and Lemma 15 assumes V_h is decreasing without proving this for the allowed parameter range. These points look potentially repairable, but the current manuscript does not yet provide a rigorous basis for its central sample-complexity theorem.

Necessary: The broad empirical outperformance claim is supported only by one one-dimensional, two-objective synthetic setting sampled from the assumed independent GP prior. There is no adaptive-versus-uniform discretization ablation, the closest PAL baseline is omitted, and accuracy and coverage are averaged into one number rather than reported separately. The manuscript also does not explain how the returned union of continuous cells is discretized for evaluation. Either narrow the empirical claims to this illustrative setting or add varied dimensions, dependent-output problems, standard benchmarks, and separately reported metrics.

Necessary: Correct specification and usability issues include defining maximum information gain as a maximum over observation vectors rather than queried design sequences, inconsistent zero/one-based observation indexing in Algorithm 1, an incorrect child-index range in the prose, and delayed or ambiguous definitions of h_max and rate constants. These should be repaired to make the algorithm and theorem unambiguous.

Optional: Release the Adaptive epsilon-PAL implementation and full configurations; add higher-dimensional or real applications, dependent-objective experiments, hardware details, and confidence intervals that account for the five runs sharing each of ten sampled functions.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: fixed-confidence Pareto-set identification over large or continuous design spaces. The adaptive-discretization approach has an identifiable audience in multi-objective Bayesian optimization and bandit optimization.
The algorithm combines GP posterior uncertainty with within-cell variation bounds, allowing it to reason about entire regions rather than a fixed grid. Supporting dependent GP outputs is also useful.

The authors attempt a substantial theoretical treatment, including correctness, termination, information-gain and metric-dimension sample-complexity bounds. The overall proof architecture is informative even though important steps need repair.

The manuscript is generally organized and understandable, with definitions, pseudocode, illustrations, related-work comparisons, and a computational-complexity discussion. It also candidly reports the inability to obtain terminating runs for the closest ε-PAL baseline.

The experiment reports multiple metrics, 10 sampled functions with five runs each, 99% confidence intervals, four relevant baselines, and the severe runtime cost of the theoretically chosen tree depth rather than concealing that tradeoff.
weaknesses: Necessary—The central sample-complexity arguments are not established as written. Propositions 4 and 5 incorrectly infer that the terminal uncertainty is below ε from Lemma 3, which only gives a sufficient termination condition, and then conclude Pr(τ_s>T)=0 from an event concerning τ_s=T. A valid stopping-time contradiction must be supplied. Lemma 15 also defines K1 using β_{τ_s} while subsequently treating it as a constant independent of the stopping time.

Necessary—The metric-dimension proof uses the parent’s refinement inequality with the current, larger confidence parameter in Lemma 14. Refinement only establishes the inequality at the earlier refinement time, and β can subsequently increase; the displayed bound therefore does not follow. The root case also invokes an undefined parent. A proof based on inherited cumulative rectangles may be possible, but it is absent.

Necessary—Proposition 1 does not support the prominent claim that neither bound dominates. Its Ω(T) conclusion requires the amplitudes to remain bounded away from zero, but that is incompatible with the asserted Hölder control along infinitely many independent bumps accumulating in a compact space. The interval construction also omits x=0, and the proof replaces the variance after mixing by A with an unmixed amplitude. This proposition should be removed, substantially narrowed, or replaced with a valid construction.

Necessary—Several auxiliary probability arguments require correction: V_h contains log(h²) although h=0 is included; the proof of Corollary 1 asserts an equality between metric balls that generally does not hold; and Lemma 5 compares conditional entropies given two non-nested conditioning sets. Although some conclusions may be recoverable by standard variance-monotonicity and ball-inclusion arguments, the current derivations are invalid.

Necessary—The empirical accuracy metric is inconsistent or ambiguous relative to the paper’s own dominance definitions. As written, checking whether a predicted point is ε-dominated by a true Pareto point is generally trivial and is not equivalent to membership in the ε-Pareto slab. Moreover, Table 2 averages accuracy and coverage instead of reporting them separately, so neither required property nor the claimed high-probability success rate can be verified.

Necessary—The experimental evidence is too narrow for the broad superiority and efficiency claims: it uses only one one-dimensional, two-objective synthetic setting with independent outputs, does not ablate adaptive versus uniform discretization, omits the closest baseline, and does not explain how returned regions and baseline outputs are converted into comparable finite sets or report their sizes. The guarantee-preserving configuration takes over 15 hours versus 40 seconds for qNEHVI, while the fast depth-limited configurations set V_h=0 and are not covered by the theory.

Optional—Release the implementation and add correlated-output, higher-dimensional, real-world, equal-budget, set-size-controlled, and discretization-sensitivity experiments. Numerous smaller notation and prose errors should also be corrected, including maximizing information gain over observations rather than design sequences, the child-index range, variance/standard-deviation terminology, and describing a polynomial rate as exponential.

Overall, the audience-interest and communication criterion is met, but the evidence criterion remains unresolved for central theoretical and empirical claims. The core approach appears plausibly repairable, supporting leaning reject rather than outright reject.

strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable problem of interest to researchers in multi-objective Bayesian optimization: Pareto-set identification over large or continuous design spaces.

Adaptive discretization is integrated with Pareto active learning in a coherent algorithm. The intuition, phase-by-phase description, pseudocode, and diagrams make the main construction reasonably understandable.
The attempt to provide complementary information-gain and metric-dimension sample-complexity bounds is valuable, particularly because the multi-output GP model permits dependent objectives.

The experiments compare against several established methods, use multiple sampled functions and noise realizations, report runtime as well as solution quality, and expose the severe computational cost of the theoretically selected tree depth rather than concealing it.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central sample-complexity theorem is not convincingly proved as written. Among other issues, the confidence radius contains log(h^2) although levels include h=0; Lemma 11 incorrectly declares a matrix positive definite when it can only be positive semidefinite; and Lemma 14 assumes that the current beta_t^{1/2} sigma_t of a parent remains below V after an earlier refinement, even though beta_t subsequently increases. The inherited cumulative rectangles may permit a repaired argument, but that argument is absent.

Necessary: Propositions 4 and 5 make an invalid stopping-time inference: from a bound evaluated at the eventual termination time and the event tau_s=T, they conclude Pr(tau_s>T)=0. The diameter bound instead needs to be established for every pre-termination evaluation prefix and then applied at T. Related dependence of K1, K2, and H on the unknown tau_s is not reconciled with Theorem 1's description of these quantities.

Necessary: Proposition 1 does not establish its claimed linear information-gain example under the setting needed for comparison with the metric-dimension bound. The proof never constructs a compact, well-behaved finite-dimensional metric satisfying the Hölder assumption; amplitudes bounded away from zero conflict with that assumption near the accumulating design points. It also replaces the post-mixing variance sum_l a_il^2 a_jl^2 by a_ij^2 without sufficient conditions, and incorrectly calls a polynomial-in-T expression exponentially decreasing. This proposition should be rigorously replaced or its associated claims removed.

Necessary: The empirical metrics are insufficiently specified and potentially inconsistent with the theory. Table 2 averages accuracy and coverage into one number, concealing their distinct failure modes. Moreover, the stated operational test for epsilon-accuracy—being epsilon-dominated by a true-front point—does not by itself characterize membership in the defined epsilon-Pareto slab. The paper must give the exact formulas or implementation, report accuracy and coverage separately, and explain how the returned union of cells is converted into evaluated points.

Necessary unless the claims are narrowed: The broad assertion that Adaptive epsilon-PAL outperforms competing methods rests on one prior-matched, one-dimensional, two-objective synthetic setting with independent objectives. There is no higher-dimensional case, correlated-output experiment, real application, or direct adaptive-versus-uniform discretization ablation. qNEHVI is also competitive or superior under several quality/runtime comparisons. The empirical claims should be restricted to this experiment or supported more broadly.

Necessary: Practical and theoretical variants are conflated. The guaranteed setting takes roughly 15 hours, whereas the fast variants impose h_max=9 or 10 and set V_h=0 beyond that depth, thereby leaving the theorem's conditions. Claims of exceptional speed or simultaneous theoretical and practical benefit need qualification, together with evaluation-count distributions and runtime environment details.

Optional: Reproducibility and clarity would improve with released implementation code, a concrete construction of the partition tree for general metric spaces, separate notation for node sets and unions of cells, and correction of indexing errors, duplicated runtime discussion, and other typographical inconsistencies.

Overall, the idea and intended audience satisfy the interest criterion, but unresolved gaps in the main theoretical evidence and ambiguity in the empirical evaluation prevent acceptance in the present form. The work has a plausible path through repaired proofs and narrower or better-supported claims, motivating a leaning-reject rather than a categorical rejection.

strengths: The problem is important to researchers in multi-objective Bayesian optimization and pure exploration: adaptive discretization could avoid the cost of imposing a fine uniform grid. The assessment is based on the complete manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-liv55mg0/call-db09829cf3764c9880c301c75314c6d7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The proposed algorithm combines region-level GP confidence rectangles, discarding, covering, and adaptive refinement in a conceptually coherent way. The intuition, pseudocode, and illustrations make this technically involved construction relatively approachable.
Providing both information-gain and metric-dimension analyses is potentially valuable, particularly because the multi-output posterior can exploit correlations between objectives.

The experiments include several established and modern baselines, repeated trials over multiple GP draws, stricter-than-target evaluation thresholds, and a useful examination of the runtime–tree-depth tradeoff.
weaknesses: Necessary: The algorithm and theorem are not fully well-defined at their starting point. The displayed V_h contains log(h^2) while h starts at zero, and the root-node confidence bounds invoke an undefined parent and V_{-1}. In addition, the metric-dimension definition quantifies over every r>0; for a nonempty space its polynomial covering inequality cannot hold as r tends to infinity. Explicit root conventions and the standard restricted radius range are required.

Necessary: A central step supporting the metric-dimension bound is unjustified. Lemma 14 asserts that β_{τ_t}^{1/2}‖σ_{τ_t}(p(x))‖ remains below V_{h-1} merely because the parent was previously refined. The refinement condition held with the earlier value of β, whereas β subsequently increases, so the stated inequality need not persist. Lemma 15 also defines K_1 using β_{τ_s}, while Theorem 1 treats K_1 as independent of T and supplies another β_T factor. The metric-dimension sample-complexity claim therefore needs a corrected proof and consistent constants.

Necessary: Proposition 1 does not establish the claimed linear information-gain example under the paper's assumptions. Its Ω(T) conclusion requires bump variances bounded away from zero, but infinitely many mutually uncorrelated, nonvanishing bumps cannot satisfy the Hölder natural-metric condition on a compact, finite-dimensional metric space. If the amplitudes decay sufficiently for compactness, the displayed lower bound does not imply Ω(T). The construction also omits 0 from its claimed partition of [0,1], and the final statement incorrectly calls a polynomial-in-T bound exponential. Consequently, the asserted non-comparability of the two bounds is unsupported.

Necessary: Several additional proof steps require repair or fuller justification. Corollary 1 claims equality between a d-ball and an induced-metric ball when only an inclusion follows; Lemma 11 incorrectly declares a posterior-reduction matrix positive definite when it can be merely semidefinite; the termination/sample-bound propositions infer Pr(τ_s>T)=0 from an implication involving τ_s=T without presenting the needed prefix argument; and parts of Lemma 9 use an unestablished same-cell relation. Although some issues may be locally repairable, their accumulation prevents the main theorem from being convincing as submitted.

Necessary: The empirical metrics are not specified consistently with Definition 5. The stated operational test for membership in Z_ε appears to reverse or trivialize the domination relation, and Table 2 averages accuracy and coverage into one number, thereby hiding whether either required property fails. The paper should give exact finite-set computations, explain how the region-valued output is discretized, report accuracy and coverage separately, and ideally report the proportion of runs satisfying both conditions.

Necessary: The broad empirical claims are supported by only one one-dimensional, two-objective synthetic setting with independent objectives. This neither tests correlated outputs nor establishes scalability to the motivating large spaces. Moreover, the fast h_max=9 and 10 variants set V_h=0 beyond the cutoff and thus lack the stated guarantee, while the theoretically parameterized version takes over 15 hours. Claims of general superiority and exceptional efficiency should be narrowed substantially or supported with correlated and higher-dimensional tasks, matched evaluation curves, implementation details, and reproducible code.

Optional: The presentation would benefit from removing duplicated runtime discussion, correcting notation and indexing slips, separating sample efficiency from wall-clock comparisons across different software stacks, and adding ablations isolating adaptive discretization and cross-objective dependence.

strengths: The manuscript clearly motivates Pareto-set identification over continuous design spaces and presents a coherent adaptive-discretization approach of interest to researchers in Bayesian optimization and pure exploration. The reviewed source is :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-1qta84w5/call-83e615d7a8494bd8b7820f9f02b5eb40/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The algorithm combines region-level GP confidence sets, discarding, Pareto covering, and selective refinement in a principled way; the phase-by-phase explanation, pseudocode, and illustrations make the main idea understandable.

Providing both joint information-gain and metric-dimension complexity analyses is potentially valuable. In particular, the information-gain calculation explicitly accommodates dependence among objectives rather than simply analyzing independent scalar GPs.
The paper carefully defines its approximate-Pareto target and attempts to prove both soundness of the returned regions and coverage of the true Pareto front.

The experimental section includes repeated noisy trials, several established MOBO baselines, quality and coverage considerations, and a useful illustration of the computational effect of limiting tree depth.
weaknesses: Necessary: the central sample-complexity theorem is not yet established by the presented proof. Lemma 11 incorrectly claims that K_x(K+Σ)^{-1}K_xᵀ is positive definite; it can be singular or zero. More importantly, Lemma 14 applies the refinement inequality β_t^{1/2}σ_t(parent)≤V_{h-1} at a later round, although it was only known at the earlier refinement round and β_t subsequently increases. An invariant based on inherited cumulative rectangles may repair this, but that argument is absent.

Necessary: Propositions 4 and 5 make an invalid stopping-time inference: `{τ_s=T} implies {ω_{t_s}<ε}` does not imply `Pr(τ_s>T)=0`. The authors need a contradiction argument that applies the diameter bound to the state immediately before the T-th possible evaluation, together with appropriate monotonicity conditions.

Necessary: several definitions used by the theorem are formally broken. V_h contains log(h²) while h starts at zero, and the corresponding union bound sums h^{-2} from h=0. The metric-dimension definition requires its covering inequality for every r>0, which is impossible for positive dimension as r→∞; it needs a bounded-radius range. The packing proof also confuses distances r and 2r. These are repairable, but the theorem is not valid as written.

Necessary: Proposition 1 does not convincingly establish the advertised non-comparability of the two bounds. Its intervals omit x=0 despite claiming to partition [0,1]; the amplitude sequence and mixing matrix are not chosen so that the displayed variance identities and Ω(T) conclusion follow; and the claimed “suitably chosen” compact, well-behaved metric satisfying the Hölder condition is never constructed. Indeed, linear information requires amplitudes bounded away from zero, which creates infinitely many GP-metric-separated designs and appears incompatible with compactness under l≤Cd^α. The proposition needs a valid construction or the associated claim should be removed or narrowed. The statement that the metric bound decreases “exponentially” in T is also false—it is polynomial up to logarithms.

Necessary: the experiments do not support the broad claim that the method outperforms competing Pareto-identification methods. They cover only one one-dimensional, two-objective synthetic setting sampled from the method's correctly specified independent GP prior. This neither tests large or high-dimensional spaces nor the claimed advantage from dependent objectives.

Necessary: the empirical metrics and comparison protocol are insufficiently specified. Accuracy and coverage are averaged into one reported number, which can conceal failure of either requirement; the method returns continuous cells while baselines return finite sets, but the sampling used to compare those outputs is not explained. Baselines receive 100 evaluations versus roughly 35–50 for the proposed method, so neither matched-budget performance nor sample-efficiency curves are shown. Runtime comparisons across different software implementations also lack enough implementation and hardware detail to be interpretable.

Necessary: setting V_h=0 at practical depth limits removes the within-cell variation allowance on which the coverage proof depends. These fast variants should be explicitly presented as heuristics without the theorem's guarantee, and their claimed accuracy advantage should be separated from conclusions about the theoretically configured algorithm, which takes over 15 hours in the reported experiment.

Optional: reproducibility and usefulness would improve with released implementation details, separate accuracy and coverage tables, budget-versus-quality curves, ablations of adaptive refinement, and experiments varying input dimension, number and correlation of objectives, noise, kernel misspecification, and real-world tasks. Numerous indexing and notation errors—such as observing y_0 at initialization and an incorrect child-index range in the prose—should also be corrected.
